Indeed. Adversity is a critical component in the human experience. It is a silly example, but think of how many artists make their best work when they are unknown and hungry, sometimes with literally nothing to their name. They get fame and success and suddenly the magic is gone. In our own, much more mundane lives, we work ourselves into places of luxuriant indolence (I certainly feel like I have), and so much of what once brought us joy is now lost. One would do well to remember of course, that what satisfies us is always a moving target. What brought you contentment in the studio apartment days may no more content you now than the playground which brought you the same contentment as a child.

One wonders, is the modern difficulty more in capturing what pleases us, or simply uncovering what that satisfaction requires? Ultimately, while we all must seek, we can never find it for long, for then we stop moving. The opioid addict, lost in his or her perfumed clouds of bliss, finds pure chemically-induced contentment. Yet, even if one could assure an uninterrupted, lifetime supply of such drugs, who among us would long to occupy such a place? Discontentment drives us forward, to be the enterprising species which we are (though some small solace that is). At any rate, this is why I find the concept of “happiness” so very suspect. It is so intangible, so illusory, it keeps people on the hedonic treadmill all their lives. Sometimes the trick is not finding ways to reach the goal, but changing what the goal even is, but I digress. I’m certainly rambling here. I’m becoming as interested in the framing of the problem and potential solutions as I am in the posited problem itself...
